title: A Veil for the Choir Anew
premise: The Guild of the Ledgered Veil survives by trading in impossible things—borrowed years, unspoken names, griefs sold by weight—and Noor Kavanagh, its youngest and most invisible member, keeps accounts no one else can read. When a child arrives speaking a language older than kingdoms, Noor discovers the child is a fragment of King Aldric's true self, cast out by the thing wearing his crown, and that the guild's long invisibility was purchased with the king's stolen memory. To save the free cities from the usurper's armies, Noor must lead the guild's last members into the capital, restore Aldric to himself, and pay the ledger's price: their own memories of everyone they love. In the end, Noor unmakes the crown-thing at the cost of forgetting the guild entirely, and begins again as a stranger welcomed through the guild's door.
about_author: I. M. Fairweather is the pen name of a former archivist who claims to have catalogued three collections that officially never existed. They write fantasy about paperwork, memory, and the quiet violence of institutions.

chapters.title: Entries in a Dying Hand
chapters.summary: Noor Kavanagh, POV. Noor catalogs the guild's dwindling inventory of impossible goods while the senior members argue over whether to dissolve. The emotional beat is weary devotion: Noor loves an institution that has forgotten them, establishing the theme of memory as currency.

chapters.title: The Child Who Knocked Twice
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. A mud-caked child arrives speaking a language that predates kingdoms; the guild's wards recognize it as pre-Founding speech. The beat is uncanny wonder curdling into fear when the child writes Noor's secret name in the dust—a name Noor never told anyone.

chapters.title: What the Veil Was For
chapters.summary: Guildmistress Sable Vane, POV. Sable reveals fragments of the guild's founding bargain: invisibility bought with a king's memory. The beat is reluctant confession, as Sable decides the child means the debt has come due and the veil is failing.

chapters.title: Ledger of Borrowed Years
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. Decoding the oldest ledgers, Noor finds entries signed in the child's hand, dated centuries ago. The beat is vertigo—the guild's survival has been an installment plan on someone else's soul, and Noor's own apprenticeship is listed as collateral.

chapters.title: Armies on the Salt Road
chapters.summary: Captain Ede Rusk of the free cities' militia, POV. Ede watches the usurper's host burn a border town that traded in the guild's wares. The beat is dread and resolve, showing the external stakes closing in while the guild debates internally.

chapters.title: The Thing Wearing His Crown
chapters.summary: King Aldric, POV. Inside the palace, Aldric experiences hours missing from his life and a cold intelligence speaking through his decrees. The beat is horror of self-estrangement—he signs orders he cannot remember giving, marching armies toward the free cities.

chapters.title: A Price Quoted in Grief
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. The guild votes to act; the ledger quotes the cost of restoring the king: one keeper's every memory of love. Noor volunteers before understanding what it means. The beat is impulsive courage shadowed by the older members' knowing silence.

chapters.title: Teaching the Child to Be a Boy
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. Traveling toward the capital, Noor teaches the child—Wren—to eat, joke, and lie like a living boy, while Wren recites Aldric's scattered memories in his sleep. The beat is tender found-family warmth that raises the price of the coming sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Second Fare
chapters.summary: Sable Vane, POV. At a river crossing, a guild defector turned usurper's agent offers Sable her old life back if she surrenders Wren. The beat is temptation and refusal; Sable kills the ferryman's ghost to keep the crossing secret, hardening her resolve.

chapters.title: Markets Where Nothing Is Sold
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. In a neutral city, Noor trades favors with other hidden guilds and learns the crown-thing is one of seven veils gone wrong. The beat is widening scope: this is not one kingdom's curse but a systemic rot the guilds enabled.

chapters.title: Ede's Impossible Bargain
chapters.summary: Ede Rusk, POV. Outnumbered, Ede buys a single borrowed hour of perfect courage for her militia, paying with her memory of her dead brother. The beat is tragic pragmatism, dramatizing the theme that survival always costs something irreplaceable.

chapters.title: The Gate That Remembers Names
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. The party infiltrates the capital through a gate that demands true names; Wren's pre-Founding tongue opens it, but the gate memorizes Noor. The beat is tense triumph undercut by the sense of being written into a larger ledger.

chapters.title: Audience with a Hollow Man
chapters.summary: Aldric, POV. Wren is brought before the court as a foundling singer; Aldric feels his missing self across the throne room. The beat is aching recognition—the hollow king weeps without knowing why, and the crown-thing notices.

chapters.title: Sable's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Sable Vane, POV. The crown-thing traps Sable and offers to erase the guild's debt if she betrays Noor. She falsifies the master ledger to buy time instead, dying under the wardens' knives with her final entry unfinished. The beat is defiant sacrifice.

chapters.title: Reading by Candlelight of Enemies
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. Grieving Sable, Noor deciphers her forged entries and learns the crown-thing's true name is buried in the guild's first book—in language only Wren can speak. The beat is sorrow transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Usurper's Armies Reach the Walls
chapters.summary: Ede Rusk, POV. The free cities' walls are breached as Ede spends the last of her borrowed hour. The beat is desperate, costly heroism; she sends word to Noor that whatever happens in the palace must happen tonight.

chapters.title: Unbinding the King
chapters.summary: Noor and Wren, alternating POV. In the throne room, Wren speaks the first name and the crown-thing unmakes itself from Aldric—but tries to take Wren with it. Noor interposes the ledger itself as collateral. The beat is terrifying, luminous climax.

chapters.title: The Price Collected
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. The ledger collects: Noor's memories of the guild, of Wren, of everyone loved, peel away page by page. The beat is devastating loss rendered gently—Noor forgets even why they are crying, holding a boy whose name means nothing now.

chapters.title: A Kingdom Put Back Together
chapters.summary: Aldric, POV. Whole again, Aldric halts the armies and opens negotiations with the free cities, haunted by gratitude he cannot aim at anyone. The beat is sober restoration; power regained is power distrusted.

chapters.title: Empty Ledgers, Open Door
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren, restored as heir and fragment made whole, keeps vigil over Noor, who remembers nothing of the guild or him. The beat is bittersweet hope—love tested against erasure, choosing to begin again anyway.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. Drawn by nothing they can name, Noor knocks twice on the door of a guild they've never heard of. The beat is circular grace: the story ends where it began, but this time the door opens onto welcome rather than duty.

chapters.title: First Entry, New Hand
chapters.summary: Noor, POV. Taking up the pen as the guild's newest keeper, Noor writes a first entry in a fresh ledger: 'A child arrived today who seems to know me.' The beat is quiet renewal—memory lost, but the capacity for it, and for love, intact.
